Many questions about a graph are questions about a *shape*: who acted in a movie that someone else
directed, which pairs of nodes point at each other, which accounts send money to an account that
sends it straight back. Cypher, the query language of Neo4j and of the openCypher standard, writes
such a shape as ASCII art, `(p:Person)-[:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie)`, with nodes in parentheses and
relationships as arrows. EdgeCase reads a large part of Cypher's query language and finds the
matches in its own graphs, with three methods:

| Method | Gives | Use it to |
|---|---|---|
| [`match()`](../reference/Graph.match.qmd) | a Polars DataFrame, one row per match | look at the matches, aggregate them, or join them to node and edge data |
| [`select_match()`](../reference/Graph.select_match.qmd) | the graph, with the matched nodes or edges selected | act on the matches with the `_ws` methods: tag, delete, extract |
| [`count_matches()`](../reference/Graph.count_matches.qmd) | an integer | count motifs, check that a pattern occurs, write tests |

Queries only read the graph. To *build* a graph from Cypher `CREATE` statements, use
[`from_cypher()`](../reference/from_cypher.qmd), and to write one out for a graph database, use
[`to_cypher()`](../reference/to_cypher.qmd).

## A movie graph

The examples on this page use a small graph of actors, directors, and films, written in Cypher and
loaded with `from_cypher()`:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec

movies = ec.from_cypher("""
CREATE (keanu:Person {name: 'Keanu Reeves', born: 1964}),
       (carrie:Person {name: 'Carrie-Anne Moss', born: 1967}),
       (laurence:Person {name: 'Laurence Fishburne', born: 1961}),
       (hugo:Person {name: 'Hugo Weaving', born: 1960}),
       (lana:Person {name: 'Lana Wachowski', born: 1965}),
       (lilly:Person {name: 'Lilly Wachowski', born: 1967}),
       (chad:Person {name: 'Chad Stahelski', born: 1968}),
       (halle:Person {name: 'Halle Berry', born: 1966}),
       (matrix:Movie {title: 'The Matrix', released: 1999}),
       (reloaded:Movie {title: 'The Matrix Reloaded', released: 2003}),
       (atlas:Movie {title: 'Cloud Atlas', released: 2012}),
       (wick:Movie {title: 'John Wick', released: 2014}),
       (wick3:Movie {title: 'John Wick: Chapter 3', released: 2019}),
       (keanu)-[:ACTED_IN {roles: ['Neo']}]->(matrix),
       (carrie)-[:ACTED_IN {roles: ['Trinity']}]->(matrix),
       (laurence)-[:ACTED_IN {roles: ['Morpheus']}]->(matrix),
       (hugo)-[:ACTED_IN {roles: ['Agent Smith']}]->(matrix),
       (keanu)-[:ACTED_IN {roles: ['Neo']}]->(reloaded),
       (carrie)-[:ACTED_IN {roles: ['Trinity']}]->(reloaded),
       (laurence)-[:ACTED_IN {roles: ['Morpheus']}]->(reloaded),
       (hugo)-[:ACTED_IN {roles: ['Agent Smith']}]->(reloaded),
       (hugo)-[:ACTED_IN {roles: ['Bill Smoke', 'Nurse Noakes']}]->(atlas),
       (halle)-[:ACTED_IN {roles: ['Luisa Rey', 'Jocasta Ayrs']}]->(atlas),
       (keanu)-[:ACTED_IN {roles: ['John Wick']}]->(wick),
       (keanu)-[:ACTED_IN {roles: ['John Wick']}]->(wick3),
       (halle)-[:ACTED_IN {roles: ['Sofia']}]->(wick3),
       (laurence)-[:ACTED_IN {roles: ['The Bowery King']}]->(wick3),
       (lana)-[:DIRECTED]->(matrix), (lilly)-[:DIRECTED]->(matrix),
       (lana)-[:DIRECTED]->(reloaded), (lilly)-[:DIRECTED]->(reloaded),
       (lana)-[:DIRECTED]->(atlas), (lilly)-[:DIRECTED]->(atlas),
       (chad)-[:DIRECTED]->(wick), (chad)-[:DIRECTED]->(wick3),
       (keanu)-[:KNOWS]->(carrie), (keanu)-[:KNOWS]->(chad), (laurence)-[:KNOWS]->(hugo)
""", graph_name="Movies")

movies.get_node_df()
```

`from_cypher()` maps Cypher's vocabulary onto EdgeCase's. Each node's Cypher label (`:Person` or
`:Movie`) became its `type`, each relationship type (`:ACTED_IN`) became an edge's `rel`, and the
other properties became attributes. The `name` property became the node label, and the movies,
which have a `title` rather than a `name`, were labelled with their variable names instead.

## A first query

`match()` finds every way a pattern fits the graph. Each match is one row, and each named variable
is a column holding the ID of the node or edge it matched:

```{python}
movies.match("MATCH (p:Person)-[r:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie)")
```

There are fourteen acting credits, so fourteen rows. The ID columns are exact and join directly
onto the node and edge tables, but they're hard to read; `use_labels=True` shows node labels
instead:

```{python}
movies.match("MATCH (p:Person)-[:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie {title: 'Cloud Atlas'})", use_labels=True)
```

The property map `{title: 'Cloud Atlas'}` restricts `m` to one movie. More general conditions go
in a `WHERE` clause, and a `RETURN` clause chooses the columns, which can include properties:

```{python}
movies.match(
    "MATCH (p:Person)-[r:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie) WHERE m.released < 2000 "
    "RETURN p.name, r.roles, m.title"
)
```

Values from outside the query go in through `params=`, as `$name` parameters. They need no quoting
or escaping, which makes them the safe way to put user input into a query, and they let one query
string be reused with different values:

```{python}
movies.match(
    "MATCH (p:Person) WHERE p.born >= $year RETURN p.name, p.born ORDER BY p.born",
    params={"year": 1966},
)
```

## How queries read an EdgeCase graph

A query reads a graph the same way `from_cypher()` writes one, so queries work on graphs built in
any way, not only from Cypher:

| In the query | Reads |
|---|---|
| `(n:Person)` | nodes whose `type` is `"Person"`, or a list that contains it |
| `(n:Person:Actor)` | nodes that have both types (`type` is a list) |
| `(n:Person\|Movie)` | nodes that have either type |
| `-[r:KNOWS]->` | edges whose `rel` is `"KNOWS"` |
| `-[r:KNOWS\|LIKES]->` | edges with either `rel` |
| `n.name` | the `name` attribute, or the node's label if it has none (see `label_key=`) |
| `r.weight` | the edge weight |
| `n.age`, `r.since` | the attribute of that name; a missing attribute is `null` |
| `(n {age: 30})` | the same as `WHERE n.age = 30` |
| `id(n)`, `id(r)` | the node or edge ID, as in the `match()` table |
| `type(r)` | the edge's `rel` |
| `labels(n)` | the node's `type`, as a list |

Here is a graph built with ordinary EdgeCase methods, queried with Cypher:

```{python}
people = (
    ec.Graph(directed=True)
    .add_node("Ann", type="Person", age=31)
    .add_node("Bob", type="Person", age=27)
    .add_node("Cy", type="Person")
    .add_edge("Ann", "Bob", rel="KNOWS", since=2019)
    .add_edge("Bob", "Cy", rel="KNOWS", since=2023)
)

people.match("MATCH (a:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->(b) WHERE r.since < 2020 RETURN a.name, b.name, b.age")
```

Ann, Bob, and Cy have no `name` attribute, so `a.name` and `b.name` read their labels.
`label_key=` chooses which property falls back to the label (`"name"` by default), and
`label_key=None` makes every property read only attributes.

The two functions `labels()` and `type()` are handy for getting an overview of an unfamiliar graph,
combined with the aggregation described below:

```{python}
movies.match("MATCH ()-[r]->() RETURN type(r) AS rel, count(*) AS edges ORDER BY edges DESC")
```

## Patterns

A pattern is a chain of nodes and relationships, and can be as long as needed. Variables are
optional, so nodes and relationships that only shape the pattern can stay anonymous. Here are the
directors whose films Keanu Reeves acted in:

```{python}
movies.match(
    "MATCH (:Person {name: 'Keanu Reeves'})-[:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie)<-[:DIRECTED]-(d:Person) "
    "RETURN DISTINCT d.name"
)
```

Arrows can point either way (`-->` or `<--`), and `--` matches a relationship in either direction.
The long forms `-[r]->`, `-[r:TYPE]->`, `-[:A|B]->`, and `-[r {since: 2020}]->` name the
relationship, restrict its type, or test its properties.

### Several patterns

Patterns separated by commas are matched together and share their variables, which is how to
describe shapes that branch or close into cycles. A variable used twice refers to the same node, so
this finds the actors who worked with both the Wachowskis and Chad Stahelski:

```{python}
movies.match(
    "MATCH (lana:Person {name: 'Lana Wachowski'})-[:DIRECTED]->(m1)<-[:ACTED_IN]-(a), "
    "      (a)-[:ACTED_IN]->(m2)<-[:DIRECTED]-(:Person {name: 'Chad Stahelski'}) "
    "RETURN DISTINCT a.name"
)
```

### Variable-length relationships

`-[*]->` matches a chain of one or more relationships, and bounds limit its length: `*2` means
exactly two, `*1..3` one to three, `*..3` up to three, and `*0..` allows zero, which makes both ends
the same node. Types and properties apply to every relationship in the chain. In the movie graph,
two `ACTED_IN` steps lead from an actor through a film to a co-star:

```{python}
movies.match(
    "MATCH (:Person {name: 'Halle Berry'})-[:ACTED_IN*2]-(costar:Person) "
    "RETURN DISTINCT costar.name"
)
```

Variable-length relationships come into their own on hierarchies, where the chain can be any
length. In this reporting structure, an unbounded `*` finds everyone under Ada, however far down,
and `size(r)`, the number of edges in the chain, gives the number of levels between them:

```{python}
org = ec.from_cypher("""
CREATE (ada:Person {name: 'Ada'}), (ben:Person {name: 'Ben'}), (cai:Person {name: 'Cai'}),
       (dee:Person {name: 'Dee'}), (eli:Person {name: 'Eli'}), (fay:Person {name: 'Fay'}),
       (ben)-[:REPORTS_TO]->(ada), (cai)-[:REPORTS_TO]->(ada),
       (dee)-[:REPORTS_TO]->(ben), (eli)-[:REPORTS_TO]->(dee), (fay)-[:REPORTS_TO]->(cai)
""")

org.match(
    "MATCH (e:Person)-[r:REPORTS_TO*]->(:Person {name: 'Ada'}) "
    "RETURN e.name AS employee, size(r) AS levels ORDER BY levels, employee"
)
```

Ben and Cai report to Ada directly, Dee and Fay through one manager, and Eli through two.

The variable of a variable-length relationship holds the list of edges along the chain, so in a
table without `RETURN` its column holds lists of edge IDs. Without an upper bound, the number of
chains can grow very quickly on dense graphs, so give one when the graph isn't a hierarchy.

### Path variables and shortest paths

A *path variable* names a whole match: `p = (a)-[:KNOWS*]->(b)` binds `p` to the path from `a` to
`b`. The functions `length(p)` (the number of relationships), `nodes(p)`, and `relationships(p)`
take it apart.

`shortestPath()` matches one shortest path between each pair of end nodes, and `allShortestPaths()`
every path of that least length. Together with path variables they answer "how are these two
connected?" questions. Here is the closest connection between Halle Berry and Carrie-Anne Moss,
following relationships of any type in either direction:

```{python}
movies.match(
    "MATCH p = shortestPath((:Person {name: 'Halle Berry'})-[*]-(:Person {name: 'Carrie-Anne Moss'})) "
    "RETURN length(p) AS hops, nodes(p) AS route",
    use_labels=True,
)["route"].to_list()
```

Halle Berry appeared in *John Wick: Chapter 3* (`wick3`) with Keanu Reeves, who knows Carrie-Anne
Moss. Restricting the path to `ACTED_IN` relationships leaves only routes through shared films,
and `allShortestPaths()` lists all of them:

```{python}
movies.match(
    "MATCH p = allShortestPaths("
    "  (:Person {name: 'Halle Berry'})-[:ACTED_IN*]-(:Person {name: 'Carrie-Anne Moss'})) "
    "RETURN length(p) AS hops, nodes(p) AS route",
    use_labels=True,
)
```

Through films alone, the two are four steps apart, by six different routes. For shortest paths
that use edge weights, or for path computations over a whole graph, see
[Paths and distances](12-paths.qmd).

## Filtering with `WHERE`

`WHERE` supports most of the conditions found in Cypher:

- comparisons (`=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`) and chains such as `1962 < p.born <= 1965`,
- logic with `AND`, `OR`, `XOR`, `NOT`, and parentheses,
- `IS NULL`, `IS NOT NULL`, and `IN [...]` (or `IN $list`),
- string tests with `STARTS WITH`, `ENDS WITH`, `CONTAINS`, and `=~`, a regular expression that
  must match the whole string,
- label tests such as `n:Person` or `n:A|B`, and
- the functions `id()`, `type()`, `labels()`, `size()`, `toLower()`, `toUpper()`, `exists()`,
  `length()`, `nodes()`, and `relationships()`.

Literals can be numbers, strings, `true`, `false`, `null`, or lists. This finds the roles in which
one actor played more than one character, a feature of *Cloud Atlas*:

```{python}
movies.match(
    "MATCH (p:Person)-[r:ACTED_IN]->(m) WHERE size(r.roles) > 1 RETURN p.name, r.roles, m.title"
)
```

### Missing values

A comparison with a missing property gives `null` rather than `true` or `false`, and `WHERE` keeps a
row only when its condition is `true`. A row is therefore dropped both when its condition is false
and when the condition can't be decided. In the `people` graph, Cy has no `age`, so Cy is neither
30 or over:

```{python}
people.match("MATCH (n) WHERE n.age >= 30 RETURN n.name")
```

nor under 30:

```{python}
people.match("MATCH (n) WHERE NOT n.age >= 30 RETURN n.name")
```

Use `IS NULL` to find the missing values. Values of different types compare as unequal and can't be
ordered, so `'3' < 4` is `null`, and a pattern property such as `{age: null}` never matches.

## Shaping the results

### `RETURN`

`RETURN` lists the columns of the result, in order. Each column is an expression: a variable, a
property, a function call such as `toLower(p.name)` or `length(path)`, a comparison, or a list such
as `[p.name, p.born]`. `AS` names a column, and without it, a property's column is named after the
variable and key (`"p.name"`), and anything else after the expression as written. `RETURN *`
returns every named variable, and `RETURN DISTINCT` drops repeated rows.

Without `RETURN`, `match()` returns one column per named variable, as in the first examples on this
page.

### Aggregation

The aggregating functions `count()`, `collect()`, `sum()`, `avg()`, `min()`, and `max()` fold many
rows into one. The columns of `RETURN` that don't aggregate are the grouping keys, so this counts
the films of each actor:

```{python}
movies.match(
    "MATCH (p:Person)-[:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie) "
    "RETURN p.name AS actor, count(*) AS films ORDER BY films DESC, actor"
)
```

`collect()` gathers the values of a group into a list, so a whole cast fits in one row:

```{python}
movies.match(
    "MATCH (p:Person)-[:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie) "
    "RETURN m.title AS movie, m.released AS year, collect(p.name) AS cast ORDER BY year"
)
```

`DISTINCT` inside an aggregating function folds each different value once. A director who made
several films with the same actor should count that actor once:

```{python}
movies.match(
    "MATCH (d:Person)-[:DIRECTED]->(:Movie)<-[:ACTED_IN]-(a:Person) "
    "RETURN d.name AS director, count(DISTINCT a) AS actors ORDER BY actors DESC, director"
)
```

With no grouping keys, the whole result folds into a single row:

```{python}
movies.match(
    "MATCH (m:Movie) RETURN count(*) AS films, min(m.released) AS first, max(m.released) AS last"
)
```

Every aggregating function skips `null` values, so `count(x)` counts the rows in which `x` isn't
`null`, while `count(*)` counts every row.

### `ORDER BY`, `SKIP`, and `LIMIT`

These follow `RETURN`, in that order. `ORDER BY` sorts by one or more expressions, each `ASC` (the
default) or `DESC`, and can use the names given with `AS`; after an aggregation or
`RETURN DISTINCT`, it can only use the returned columns. `SKIP n` drops the first `n` rows and
`LIMIT n` keeps at most `n`. Together they give "top `n`" queries, such as the pairs of actors who
appeared together most often:

```{python}
movies.match(
    "MATCH (a:Person)-[:ACTED_IN]->(m)<-[:ACTED_IN]-(b:Person) WHERE a.name < b.name "
    "RETURN a.name, b.name, count(m) AS films ORDER BY films DESC, a.name, b.name LIMIT 3"
)
```

The condition `a.name < b.name` keeps one row per pair; without it, each pair would appear twice,
once in each order, as explained in [Matching rules](#matching-rules).

Without `ORDER BY`, rows are sorted by the IDs of the named variables, in the order they first
appear in the query, so the same query on the same graph always gives the same table.

## Multi-part queries

### Several `MATCH` clauses

A query can have several `MATCH` clauses. Each one extends the rows of the clauses before it,
through their shared variables, and a `WHERE` belongs to the clause it follows. `OPTIONAL MATCH`
does the same, but keeps a row that it can't extend, with `null` in its new variables. That makes it
the way to keep the nodes for which some pattern is absent. Here everyone is listed, with the number
of films they directed, including those who directed none:

```{python}
movies.match(
    "MATCH (p:Person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[:DIRECTED]->(m) "
    "RETURN p.name, count(m) AS directed ORDER BY directed DESC, p.name"
)
```

Because `count(m)` skips `null`s, the people with no directing credit count 0.

### `WITH`

`WITH` splits a query into parts. It ends one part, lists the columns to pass on (just as `RETURN`
does), and the next part runs once for each of its rows. `WITH` can aggregate, sort, and limit, and
its own `WHERE` filters the rows after that, which makes it the way to filter on an aggregate. This
finds the actors with at least three films, then goes back to the graph to list them:

```{python}
movies.match(
    "MATCH (p:Person)-[:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie) "
    "WITH p, count(m) AS films WHERE films >= 3 "
    "MATCH (p)-[:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie) "
    "RETURN p.name, films, collect(m.title) AS titles"
)
```

The second `MATCH` starts from each actor that `WITH` passed on. A column of `WITH` that holds a
node or relationship, like `p`, can be used in later patterns, while one that holds a value, like
`films`, can be used in expressions. The next part sees only the columns `WITH` lists, so `m` from
the first part is gone, and the second `MATCH` binds a new `m`.

Combining `OPTIONAL MATCH` with `WITH` expresses absence directly. These are the people who never
acted in any of the films:

```{python}
movies.match(
    "MATCH (p:Person) OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[r:ACTED_IN]->() "
    "WITH p, count(r) AS roles WHERE roles = 0 "
    "RETURN p.name"
)
```

## Working with the table

The result of `match()` is an ordinary Polars DataFrame, so anything that Cypher can't express is
one Polars step away. The ID columns join directly onto `get_node_df()` and `get_edge_df()`:

```{python}
import polars as pl

credits = movies.match("MATCH (p:Person)-[r:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie)")
nodes = movies.get_node_df()

(
    credits
    .join(nodes.select("id", "label", "born").rename({"id": "p", "label": "actor"}), on="p")
    .join(nodes.select("id", "released").rename({"id": "m"}), on="m")
    .with_columns(age=pl.col("released") - pl.col("born"))
    .group_by("actor")
    .agg(pl.col("age").min().alias("youngest"), pl.col("age").max().alias("oldest"))
    .sort("actor")
)
```

The age of each actor at each release needs arithmetic, which isn't part of the supported Cypher,
so the query finds the credits and Polars does the rest.

## Acting on the matches

`select_match()` selects what the matches bound. By default it selects every node of every match,
anonymous ones included; `select=` names the variables to select instead, and a relationship
variable selects edges. The selection then feeds the `_ws` methods described in
[Selections](08-selections.qmd):

```{python}
(
    movies
    .select_match("MATCH (p:Person)-[:DIRECTED]->(:Movie)", select="p")
    .set_node_attrs_ws(director=True)
    .clear_selection()
    .get_node_df()
    .select("label", "director")
    .head(8)
)
```

The new attribute is `null` for the people who directed nothing, since `set_node_attrs_ws()` only
touched the selected nodes. Selecting a relationship variable selects edges, here the acting credits
of the films released after 2010:

```{python}
movies.select_match(
    "MATCH (:Person)-[r:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie) WHERE m.released > 2010",
    select="r",
    set_op="replace",
)
movies.get_edge_df_ws()
```

The selection combines with the current one through `set_op=`, as in every other `select_*`
method, and `select_match()` takes no `RETURN`, since `select=` chooses what to select. A selection
is a set, so it loses the pairing within each match: after selecting `a` and `b` from
`(a)-[:KNOWS]->(b)`, there's no telling who knows whom. Use `match()` when the pairs matter.

## Counting matches

`count_matches()` gives the number of rows that `match()` would return, without building the table:

```{python}
movies.count_matches("MATCH (:Person)-[:ACTED_IN]->(:Movie)")
```

It's the natural tool for counting motifs, the small patterns whose frequency characterizes a
network. Counts follow Cypher's matching rules, which matter for symmetric patterns, as the next
section explains.

## Matching rules

The matcher follows Cypher's rules, which can surprise people who know subgraph isomorphism.

**Edges are distinct, nodes need not be.** Within one clause, each edge is used at most once, but a
node can appear more than once. So `(a)-->(b)-->(a)` finds 2-cycles, using a different edge on the
way back, and it finds each one twice, once from each end:

```{python}
loops = (
    ec.Graph(directed=True)
    .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"])
    .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "B"), ("A", "D"), ("B", "E"),
                ("C", "F"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "D"), ("E", "F")])
)

loops.match("MATCH (a)-->(b)-->(a)", use_labels=True)
```

A condition that orders the two ends keeps one row per cycle:

```{python}
loops.count_matches("MATCH (a)-->(b)-->(a) WHERE id(a) < id(b)")
```

**`distinct_nodes=True`** makes the nodes of a match distinct too, anonymous nodes included, as in
a subgraph isomorphism. A path of two edges, `(a)-->(b)-->(c)`, can come back to `a` by default,
but not with `distinct_nodes=True`:

```{python}
(
    loops.count_matches("MATCH (a)-->(b)-->(c)"),
    loops.count_matches("MATCH (a)-->(b)-->(c)", distinct_nodes=True),
)
```

The four paths that return to their start are the four rows of the 2-cycle query above.

**Undirected graphs.** In an undirected graph, every relationship matches in either direction, so
`-->`, `<--`, and `--` mean the same, and one edge matches `(x)--(y)` twice, once each way:

```{python}
path = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]).add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")])
path.match("MATCH (x)--(y)", use_labels=True)
```

**Parallel edges and self-loops.** Each of several parallel edges gives its own match, and a
self-loop matches `(a)-->(a)`.

**`limit=`.** The `limit=` argument of `match()` stops the search once it has found that many rows,
which is the fastest way to check whether a pattern occurs at all. It caps the work rather than
choosing the top rows, so the table holds the first rows *found*. For the top rows of the full
result, use `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` in the query.

## What isn't supported

EdgeCase supports Cypher's reading queries, not its writing ones. Anything outside the supported
subset raises a `ValueError` that names the problem and gives its line and column:

```{python}
try:
    movies.match("MATCH (p:Person) SET p.checked = true")
except ValueError as error:
    print(error)
```

The common cases, and what to use instead:

| Cypher | Instead |
|---|---|
| `CREATE`, `MERGE`, `SET`, `DELETE`, `REMOVE` | `from_cypher()` to build a graph, and `select_match()` followed by the `_ws` methods to change one |
| arithmetic, such as `m.released - p.born` | compute in Polars on the `match()` table |
| `CASE`, list comprehensions, `coalesce()`, and other functions | compute in Polars |
| pattern predicates, such as `WHERE NOT (p)-->()` | `OPTIONAL MATCH` with `WITH ... WHERE count(...) = 0`, as shown above |
| `UNION` | run two queries and use `pl.concat()` |
| `UNWIND`, `CALL`, and procedures | Python code around the query, or EdgeCase's own methods |

A Cypher pattern is one way to describe a shape. The other is to build the shape as a small
EdgeCase graph and search for it with
[`subgraph_isomorphisms()`](../reference/Graph.subgraph_isomorphisms.qmd). That's the better fit
when the pattern is itself data (loaded from a file, generated, or too large to write out), when
matches must be *induced* (with no extra edges among the matched nodes), or when each symmetric
copy should be found only once. Cypher is the better fit when the pattern has conditions on
properties, or when the result should be a table. [Clustering and motifs](15-clustering-and-motifs.qmd)
has more on subgraph search.

## Exchanging graphs with Cypher databases

`from_cypher()` reads any number of `CREATE` clauses, separated by `;` if need be, with `//` and
`/* */` comments, from a string or from a file given as a `Path`. `to_cypher()` does the reverse,
writing a graph as a single `CREATE` statement that loads it into Neo4j, Memgraph, or any other
Cypher database:

```{python}
print(ec.to_cypher(org))
```

Each node gets a variable (`n1`, `n2`, and so on, in ID order), its label as the `name` property,
and its type as its Cypher labels, and each edge its `rel` as the relationship type. Edges without
a `rel` get `default_rel=` (`"RELATED_TO"` by default), since Cypher requires a type for every
relationship. Pass a path as `filepath=` to write the statement to a file as well.
[File formats](27-file-formats.qmd) covers the other formats EdgeCase reads and writes.

## Performance

The matcher plans an order for the pattern's nodes and relationships, then searches: it starts
by scanning the graph's nodes for the first one, and extends each partial match one edge at a time,
checking every condition as soon as the variables it reads are bound. A few habits keep it fast:

- **Give it a good place to start.** The search starts at the most constrained node: one with an
  `id()` condition, then one with a property equality, then one with a type. A query that begins at
  a rare node, such as `(m:Movie {title: $title})`, rejects most of the graph at the first step.
- **Name nodes by ID when you can.** `WHERE id(n) = $id` and `WHERE id(n) IN $ids` go straight to
  those nodes, without scanning the others.
- **Join conditions with `AND`.** Each part of an `AND` is checked as soon as its own variables are
  bound, while an `OR` that spans several variables waits for all of them.
- **Count rather than tabulate.** `count_matches()` and `select_match()` skip building the table.
- **Stop early.** `match(limit=n)` ends the search after `n` rows.
- **Bound variable-length relationships.** An unbounded `*` on a dense graph can have an enormous
  number of matches.
- **Mind symmetric patterns.** `(a)--(b)--(c)` in a dense graph has many matches, each found twice;
  a condition such as `WHERE id(a) < id(c)` keeps one of each.
